title: AP Biology — Chapter 13 (meiosis and heredity)
source: Carter's Ch 13 guide: her slide deck slides 1-51, his spoken priority list, plus the Mendel/Hardy-Weinberg half of the Fri 11/13 quiz. Refresh this file when the unit changes.

questions.stem: A human sperm is found to carry both an X and a Y chromosome, along with 22 autosomes. Which meiotic error most directly explains this sperm?
questions.correct: Nondisjunction of the X and Y homologs during meiosis I.
distractors: Nondisjunction of sister chromatids during meiosis II.
Failure of cytokinesis after meiosis II.
Fertilization of an egg by two sperm.
questions.why: X and Y are homologs and normally separate in meiosis I, so a sperm carrying both reflects meiosis I nondisjunction, not meiosis II sister-chromatid failure.
options: Nondisjunction of the X and Y homologs during meiosis I.
Failure of cytokinesis after meiosis II.
Fertilization of an egg by two sperm.
Nondisjunction of sister chromatids during meiosis II.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte completes meiosis I. The first polar body does not divide, but the secondary oocyte is fertilized and completes meiosis II. How many cells are produced, and what is their chromosome number?
questions.correct: One ovum and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
distractors: One ovum and one polar body, each with 23 chromosomes.
Two ova and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum with 46 chromosomes and two polar bodies with 23 chromosomes.
questions.why: The first polar body persists as a haploid cell, and meiosis II adds a second polar body, leaving one haploid ovum with 23 chromosomes.
options: One ovum and one polar body, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
Two ova and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum with 46 chromosomes and two polar bodies with 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte has genotype AaBb, with the A and B genes on different chromosome pairs. After meiosis I, the secondary oocyte carries A and b. Ignoring crossing over, what does the first polar body carry?
questions.correct: a and B, because homologs of both pairs segregated to opposite poles.
distractors: A and B, because the polar body receives the sister chromatids of both chromosomes.
a and b, because independent assortment randomizes which alleles stay together.
A and b, because sister chromatids separate during meiosis I.
questions.why: Meiosis I separates homologs, not sister chromatids, so the polar body receives the other homolog of each pair: a and B.
options: A and b, because sister chromatids separate during meiosis I.
a and b, because independent assortment randomizes which alleles stay together.
a and B, because homologs of both pairs segregated to opposite poles.
A and B, because the polar body receives the sister chromatids of both chromosomes.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 10 proceeds through meiosis. At anaphase I, how many chromosomes are moving toward each pole, and how many chromatids does each of those chromosomes have?
questions.correct: 5 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
distractors: 10 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
10 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
questions.why: Anaphase I separates homologs, so each pole receives one chromosome from each of the five pairs, and each chromosome is still duplicated.
options: 10 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
10 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids

questions.stem: A human male produces 400 sperm by normal meiosis. On average, how many of these sperm carry a Y chromosome?
questions.correct: 200 sperm
distractors: 0 sperm
100 sperm
400 sperm
questions.why: X and Y separate in meiosis I, so half the sperm receive Y and half receive X, giving about 200 Y-bearing sperm.
options: 200 sperm
0 sperm
400 sperm
100 sperm

questions.stem: A chloroplast is illuminated with light, and then CO2 is suddenly removed from its surroundings. Which immediate change is expected?
questions.correct: ATP and NADPH accumulate, and O2 production continues briefly because the light reactions do not require CO2.
distractors: O2 production stops immediately because CO2 is the final electron acceptor.
ATP and NADPH production stops immediately because the Calvin cycle cannot use them.
Water splitting stops immediately because NADP+ is no longer available.
questions.why: CO2 is used in the Calvin cycle, not the light reactions; without it, ATP and NADPH build up while water splitting continues briefly.
options: O2 production stops immediately because CO2 is the final electron acceptor.
ATP and NADPH accumulate, and O2 production continues briefly because the light reactions do not require CO2.
ATP and NADPH production stops immediately because the Calvin cycle cannot use them.
Water splitting stops immediately because NADP+ is no longer available.

questions.stem: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. What is the most likely immediate effect on a respiring cell?
questions.correct: ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases because the proton gradient is lost.
distractors: O2 consumption stops immediately because electrons can no longer flow.
Glycolysis stops immediately because NADH cannot be oxidized.
ATP synthesis increases because protons reach ATP synthase more easily.
questions.why: The proton gradient drives ATP synthase; a leak dissipates it, so ATP synthesis falls even though electron transport may continue.
options: ATP synthesis increases because protons reach ATP synthase more easily.
O2 consumption stops immediately because electrons can no longer flow.
ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases because the proton gradient is lost.
Glycolysis stops immediately because NADH cannot be oxidized.

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next child will be affected?
questions.why: Both parents must be carriers, and each child has a 1/4 chance of inheriting two recessive alleles; the prior affected child does not change the next child's odds.

questions.stem: In a food chain, producers fix 50,000 kJ of energy. If 10 percent of energy is transferred to each successive trophic level, how much energy is available to the tertiary consumers?
questions.correct: 50 kJ
distractors: 500 kJ
0.5 kJ
questions.why: Energy is multiplied by 0.1 at each of three transfers: 50,000 to primary consumers is 5,000, to secondary consumers 500, and to tertiary consumers 50 kJ.
options: 50 kJ
0.5 kJ
500 kJ

questions.stem: A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from UAC (tyrosine) to UAA. What is the most likely effect on the protein produced?
questions.correct: Translation stops early because UAA is a stop codon.
distractors: One amino acid is replaced by another because the codon still specifies an amino acid.
The reading frame shifts after the mutation, changing all later amino acids.
The mRNA is not transcribed because the mutation affects the promoter.
questions.why: UAA is a nonsense codon, so the ribosome terminates translation prematurely; a substitution would require a codon that still specifies an amino acid.
options: The mRNA is not transcribed because the mutation affects the promoter.
Translation stops early because UAA is a stop codon.
One amino acid is replaced by another because the codon still specifies an amino acid.
The reading frame shifts after the mutation, changing all later amino acids.

questions.stem: One rodent species has 2n = 8 and a related species has 2n = 12; both are heterozygous at every locus. Ignoring crossing over, how many times more gamete chromosome combinations can one individual of the 12-chromosome species produce than one individual of the 8-chromosome species?
questions.correct: Four times as many, since the two species produce 64 and 16 combinations respectively
distractors: Four more combinations, because the species differ by four chromosomes in total
The same number, because both species are diploid and assort independently in the same way
Six times as many, because the larger species has six chromosome pairs
questions.why: Independent assortment yields 2^n gamete combinations, where n is the haploid number: 2^6 = 64 versus 2^4 = 16, a fourfold difference. Subtracting chromosome counts (12 - 8) mistakes chromosomes for the exponent.
options: Six times as many, because the larger species has six chromosome pairs
The same number, because both species are diploid and assort independently in the same way
Four times as many, since the two species produce 64 and 16 combinations respectively
Four more combinations, because the species differ by four chromosomes in total

questions.stem: A diploid germ cell enters meiosis without completing S phase, but its homologs still pair. Which description of a resulting tetrad is most accurate?
questions.correct: It contains two unreplicated chromosomes, so only two chromatids are present instead of four.
distractors: It contains four chromatids because homologs replicate during synapsis.
It contains two chromosomes but four centromeres because centromeres duplicate without DNA replication.
It cannot form a spindle, so homologs never pair.
questions.why: S phase produces sister chromatids; skipping it leaves one chromatid per homolog, so a tetrad has two chromatids. The wrong options assume replication occurs during synapsis or that centromeres duplicate independently.
options: It contains four chromatids because homologs replicate during synapsis.
It cannot form a spindle, so homologs never pair.
It contains two chromosomes but four centromeres because centromeres duplicate without DNA replication.
It contains two unreplicated chromosomes, so only two chromatids are present instead of four.

questions.stem: A physician examines a standard karyotype made from a person's white blood cells and sees 46 normally paired chromosomes. Why can this karyotype not reveal whether crossing over occurred during the person's meiosis?
questions.correct: It shows condensed mitotic chromosomes, not meiotic tetrads, so reciprocal exchanges leave no visible record.
distractors: Crossing over changes chromosome number, which karyotypes cannot detect.
White blood cells never undergo meiosis, so they contain no homologous chromosomes.
Crossing over only occurs in gametes, which are not present in blood.
questions.why: A karyotype uses mitotic metaphase chromosomes; crossing over happens in meiotic prophase I and is reciprocal, so it does not change chromosome number. The wrong options confuse chromosome number with exchange of segments.
options: It shows condensed mitotic chromosomes, not meiotic tetrads, so reciprocal exchanges leave no visible record.
White blood cells never undergo meiosis, so they contain no homologous chromosomes.
Crossing over only occurs in gametes, which are not present in blood.
Crossing over changes chromosome number, which karyotypes cannot detect.

questions.stem: Immediately after a human sperm and egg fuse, the zygote contains 46 chromosomes. What happens to the maternal and paternal homologs at this point?
questions.correct: They remain separate chromosomes in one nucleus and do not pair or cross over until meiosis.
distractors: They immediately pair into 23 tetrads to check for damage.
They fuse into 23 chromosomes, each containing both parental DNA.
They undergo crossing over to create new allele combinations before the first mitosis.
questions.why: Homolog pairing and crossing over occur in prophase I of meiosis, not at fertilization. The wrong options mistakenly treat fertilization as a pairing or recombination event.
options: They undergo crossing over to create new allele combinations before the first mitosis.
They remain separate chromosomes in one nucleus and do not pair or cross over until meiosis.
They fuse into 23 chromosomes, each containing both parental DNA.
They immediately pair into 23 tetrads to check for damage.

questions.stem: A human spermatogonium divides by mitosis, and one daughter enters meiosis while the other remains a stem cell. What is the main advantage of this arrangement?
questions.correct: It maintains a supply of spermatogonia while also producing gametes.
distractors: It doubles the chromosome number before meiosis begins.
It creates genetic variation by crossing over during mitosis.
It ensures every daughter cell becomes a primary oocyte.
questions.why: Mitotic division renews the stem-cell population while meiosis produces sperm. The wrong options confuse mitosis with crossing over or with meiotic chromosome reduction.
options: It creates genetic variation by crossing over during mitosis.
It ensures every daughter cell becomes a primary oocyte.
It maintains a supply of spermatogonia while also producing gametes.
It doubles the chromosome number before meiosis begins.

questions.stem: A karyotype is prepared from a normal human sperm rather than a somatic cell. Which result should the technician expect?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, with no homologous pairs present.
distractors: 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs.
23 pairs of chromosomes, including one X and one Y.
46 chromosomes, but only 22 homologous pairs.
questions.why: A sperm is haploid with 23 chromosomes, so it has no homologous pairs. The wrong options incorrectly retain the diploid pairing seen in somatic cells.
options: 23 pairs of chromosomes, including one X and one Y.
46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs.
46 chromosomes, but only 22 homologous pairs.
23 chromosomes, with no homologous pairs present.

questions.stem: Within seconds after one sperm fuses with a human egg, the egg's membrane changes and cortical granules release enzymes that prevent additional sperm from entering. Why is this block essential?
questions.correct: It prevents a zygote with extra chromosome sets, which would disrupt meiosis and development.
distractors: It prevents the egg from completing meiosis II and forming a polar body.
It ensures the zygote receives mitochondria from only the sperm.
It stops crossing over from occurring in the zygote's first mitosis.
questions.why: Polyspermy would create a triploid zygote with extra chromosome sets, disrupting development. The wrong options confuse this block with polar-body formation, mitochondria, or mitosis.
options: It prevents a zygote with extra chromosome sets, which would disrupt meiosis and development.
It prevents the egg from completing meiosis II and forming a polar body.
It ensures the zygote receives mitochondria from only the sperm.
It stops crossing over from occurring in the zygote's first mitosis.

questions.stem: In humans, a sperm contributes a haploid nucleus and a centriole, while the egg contributes a haploid nucleus plus most of the cytoplasm. Why is the egg's large cytoplasmic contribution important after fertilization?
questions.correct: It supplies nutrients and organelles that support early embryonic divisions before implantation.
distractors: It provides a second set of chromosomes that makes the zygote diploid.
It allows the zygote to skip DNA replication before its first mitosis.
It prevents independent assortment during the zygote's first meiotic division.
questions.why: The egg cytoplasm supports early development, but diploidy comes from the two haploid nuclei. The wrong options misattribute chromosome contribution or cell-cycle events to the cytoplasm.
options: It prevents independent assortment during the zygote's first meiotic division.
It supplies nutrients and organelles that support early embryonic divisions before implantation.
It provides a second set of chromosomes that makes the zygote diploid.
It allows the zygote to skip DNA replication before its first mitosis.

questions.stem: At metaphase I, chiasmata hold each pair of homologs together. What must happen to these chiasmata for anaphase I to proceed normally?
questions.correct: They must be released so the homologs can move to opposite poles.
distractors: They must duplicate so each pole receives a chiasma.
They must move to the equator and attach to spindle fibers.
They must form a synaptonemal complex between sister chromatids.
questions.why: Chiasmata are temporary links between homologs; their release allows anaphase I separation. The wrong options treat chiasmata as spindle attachments or as structures that duplicate.
options: They must duplicate so each pole receives a chiasma.
They must move to the equator and attach to spindle fibers.
They must be released so the homologs can move to opposite poles.
They must form a synaptonemal complex between sister chromatids.

questions.stem: During prophase I, two nonsister chromatids break and exchange equal segments. Why does this crossing over usually leave each chromosome with the same overall length and gene content?
questions.correct: The exchange is reciprocal, so the segments swapped between homologs are equal and replace one another.
distractors: The broken ends are repaired by DNA polymerase using the sister chromatid as a template.
The exchanged segments are immediately degraded, leaving the chromosome shorter.
Crossing over duplicates the exchanged segments, increasing gene number on both chromatids.
questions.why: Crossing over is a reciprocal exchange, so equal segments replace one another and length is conserved. The wrong options describe nonreciprocal repair, loss, or duplication.
options: The exchanged segments are immediately degraded, leaving the chromosome shorter.
Crossing over duplicates the exchanged segments, increasing gene number on both chromatids.
The broken ends are repaired by DNA polymerase using the sister chromatid as a template.
The exchange is reciprocal, so the segments swapped between homologs are equal and replace one another.

questions.stem: A cell in G1 has DNA damage. The G1/S checkpoint normally stops the cell from entering S phase. If this checkpoint fails, what is the most likely consequence?
questions.correct: The cell copies damaged DNA and may pass mutations to daughter cells.
distractors: The cell immediately enters mitosis without copying its DNA.
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during anaphase I.
The cell always undergoes apoptosis before replication.
questions.why: Checkpoint failure lets a cell replicate damaged DNA, increasing mutation risk in daughter cells. The wrong options confuse the G1/S checkpoint with mitosis or meiosis and ignore that apoptosis is not guaranteed.
options: The cell copies damaged DNA and may pass mutations to daughter cells.
The cell immediately enters mitosis without copying its DNA.
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during anaphase I.
The cell always undergoes apoptosis before replication.

questions.stem: In E. coli, a mutation prevents the lac repressor from binding the operator. If glucose is low, what happens to lac operon expression?
questions.correct: The operon is transcribed continuously, even when lactose is absent.
distractors: The operon is transcribed only when lactose is present.
The operon is never transcribed because the promoter is blocked.
The operon is transcribed only when glucose is high.
questions.why: Without repressor binding, the operator cannot block transcription, so lactose is not needed to derepress the operon. The wrong options assume the repressor is still controlling expression.
options: The operon is transcribed only when lactose is present.
The operon is transcribed continuously, even when lactose is absent.
The operon is transcribed only when glucose is high.
The operon is never transcribed because the promoter is blocked.

questions.stem: A table shows chromosome numbers in four tissues of a flowering plant: root 24, leaf 24, pollen grain 12, endosperm 36. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The endosperm is triploid, consistent with a haploid sperm nucleus fusing with two haploid polar nuclei.
distractors: The pollen grain is diploid because it has half the chromosome number of the root.
The endosperm is haploid because it is produced directly by meiosis.
The root and leaf are haploid because they contain the same number of chromosomes.
questions.why: Root and leaf are diploid (2n = 24), pollen is haploid (n = 12), and endosperm is 3n = 36 after double fertilization; the distractors confuse haploid with half and triploid with haploid.
options: The root and leaf are haploid because they contain the same number of chromosomes.
The endosperm is haploid because it is produced directly by meiosis.
The endosperm is triploid, consistent with a haploid sperm nucleus fusing with two haploid polar nuclei.
The pollen grain is diploid because it has half the chromosome number of the root.

questions.stem: Two linked genes in a plant were scored in testcrosses at two temperatures. Recombination was 8% at 15°C and 16% at 25°C. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Temperature can alter the frequency of crossing over between these linked genes.
distractors: The two genes move to different chromosomes at 25°C.
Independent assortment increases as temperature rises.
Crossing over at 25°C occurred during mitosis rather than meiosis.
questions.why: Recombination between linked genes depends on crossing over in meiosis and can be environmentally modified; the distractors confuse recombination with independent assortment or mitosis.
options: Crossing over at 25°C occurred during mitosis rather than meiosis.
The two genes move to different chromosomes at 25°C.
Independent assortment increases as temperature rises.
Temperature can alter the frequency of crossing over between these linked genes.

questions.stem: In 200 tetrads with two crossovers between the same two loci, 80 yielded two recombinant chromatids, 100 yielded three, and 20 yielded four. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Double crossovers can involve two, three, or four chromatids, so crossover number does not always equal recombinant chromatid number.
distractors: Every double crossover produces four recombinant chromatids.
Crossing over occurs only between sister chromatids.
Recombination frequency always equals the number of crossovers per tetrad.
questions.why: Two crossovers may share a chromatid, leaving some parental combinations; the distractors assume all crossovers are independent or sister-only.
options: Double crossovers can involve two, three, or four chromatids, so crossover number does not always equal recombinant chromatid number.
Recombination frequency always equals the number of crossovers per tetrad.
Crossing over occurs only between sister chromatids.
Every double crossover produces four recombinant chromatids.

questions.stem: A table records chiasmata along chromosome 3 in 100 meiocytes: 60 near the ends, 25 in the middle, and 15 near the centromere. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Crossing over is not uniformly distributed along the chromosome.
distractors: Crossing over occurs only near the chromosome ends.
Chiasmata form during anaphase I.
The centromere is the most frequent site of crossing over.
questions.why: The data show more crossovers near the ends but not exclusively there; chiasmata form in prophase I, not anaphase I.
options: Chiasmata form during anaphase I.
Crossing over is not uniformly distributed along the chromosome.
The centromere is the most frequent site of crossing over.
Crossing over occurs only near the chromosome ends.

questions.stem: A table lists four chromosome pairs from a human karyotype by length and centromere position. Pair 1 is longest and metacentric; Pair 2 is long and submetacentric; Pairs 3 and 4 are short and acrocentric. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Pairs 3 and 4 cannot be matched as homologs by length and centromere position alone; banding patterns are needed.
distractors: Pair 1 must be the X chromosome pair because it is the longest.
Pairs 3 and 4 are homologous to each other because both are acrocentric.
Centromere position alone is sufficient to identify every homologous pair.
questions.why: Many human chromosomes share size and centromere class, so karyotype pairing relies on banding; the distractors confuse similar appearance with homology.
options: Pairs 3 and 4 are homologous to each other because both are acrocentric.
Pair 1 must be the X chromosome pair because it is the longest.
Pairs 3 and 4 cannot be matched as homologs by length and centromere position alone; banding patterns are needed.
Centromere position alone is sufficient to identify every homologous pair.

questions.stem: A table lists four human ovarian cells: Cell 1 has 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids; Cell 2 has 46 and 92; Cell 3 has 23 and 46; Cell 4 has 23 and 23. Which cell is a secondary oocyte at metaphase II?
questions.correct: Cell 3, with 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
distractors: Cell 1, with 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
Cell 2, with 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
Cell 4, with 23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids.
questions.why: After meiosis I the secondary oocyte is haploid (23) but each chromosome still has two sister chromatids (46); Cell 1 is G1, Cell 2 is primary oocyte after S, and Cell 4 is an ovum.
options: Cell 4, with 23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids.
Cell 2, with 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
Cell 1, with 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
Cell 3, with 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.

questions.stem: A single meiocyte heterozygous at two linked loci produces four gametes with genotypes AB, AB, ab, and ab. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: No crossing over occurred between the two loci in this meiosis.
distractors: The two loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Crossing over occurred between sister chromatids at these loci.
The meiocyte produced four recombinant gametes.
questions.why: Only two gamete genotypes, each duplicated, indicate the alleles stayed linked; independent assortment or crossing over would produce additional recombinant types.
options: No crossing over occurred between the two loci in this meiosis.
The meiocyte produced four recombinant gametes.
The two loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Crossing over occurred between sister chromatids at these loci.

questions.stem: A table lists somatic chromosome numbers for four diploid species: Species 1 has 14, Species 2 has 28, Species 3 has 42, and Species 4 has 56. Which species produces gametes with 14 chromosomes?
questions.correct: Species 2, with 28 somatic chromosomes.
distractors: Species 1, with 14 somatic chromosomes.
Species 3, with 42 somatic chromosomes.
Species 4, with 56 somatic chromosomes.
questions.why: Gametes are haploid, so a diploid species with 28 chromosomes produces gametes with 14; the distractors mistake the somatic number for the gamete number or halve the wrong species.
options: Species 1, with 14 somatic chromosomes.
Species 2, with 28 somatic chromosomes.
Species 3, with 42 somatic chromosomes.
Species 4, with 56 somatic chromosomes.

questions.stem: A table lists chromosome contents of four human gametes: Gamete 1 has 22 autosomes + X; Gamete 2 has 22 autosomes + Y; Gamete 3 has 23 autosomes + X; Gamete 4 has 23 autosomes + Y. Which are normal sperm?
questions.correct: Gamete 1 and Gamete 2 only.
distractors: Gamete 3 and Gamete 4 only.
Gamete 1 and Gamete 3 only.
Gamete 2 and Gamete 4 only.
questions.why: A normal sperm is haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome; Gametes 3 and 4 have an extra autosome and are aneuploid.
options: Gamete 1 and Gamete 3 only.
Gamete 2 and Gamete 4 only.
Gamete 1 and Gamete 2 only.
Gamete 3 and Gamete 4 only.

questions.stem: A table shows a family: two unaffected parents have one affected daughter and one unaffected son. No other family history is given. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
questions.correct: Autosomal recessive
distractors: X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
Y-linked
questions.why: Two unaffected parents producing an affected daughter indicate a recessive allele carried by both parents; X-linked recessive is unlikely because an affected daughter would need an affected father.
options: Y-linked
Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive

questions.stem: A table shows a cross between a type A parent and a type B parent. Among their children are individuals with type A, type B, type AB, and type O blood. What are the parents' most likely genotypes?
questions.correct: IAi and IBi
distractors: IAIA and IBIB
IAi and IBIB
IAIA and IBi
questions.why: A type O child must inherit an i allele from each parent, so both parents must carry i; IAi x IBi also allows all four phenotypes.
options: IAi and IBi
IAIA and IBIB
IAIA and IBi
IAi and IBIB

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human fetus shows 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
distractors: 44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
questions.why: The 47 chromosomes split into 45 autosomes plus 2 X sex chromosomes, and chromosome 21 is an autosome; the first distractor wrongly counts the extra copy as a sex chromosome.
options: 45 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being an autosome.
47 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, with no sex chromosomes counted separately.
45 autosomes and 1 sex chromosome, with one X chromosome missing.
44 autosomes and 3 sex chromosomes, with the extra chromosome being a sex chromosome.

questions.stem: To make a karyotype, a technician arrests white blood cells in metaphase with a drug that prevents spindle fibers from separating chromosomes. Why does metaphase make homologs easiest to pair?
questions.correct: Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
distractors: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
questions.why: At metaphase chromosomes are condensed with sister chromatids still attached, allowing homologs to be paired; the first distractor confuses metaphase with anaphase separation.
options: Homologs have already separated, so each chromosome can be compared with its partner independently.
Chromosomes are condensed and still duplicated, so homologs can be matched by size, centromere position, and banding.
DNA is replicating, so each homolog is present as a single chromatid that can be aligned.
Crossing over is complete, so recombinant chromosomes can be identified by their new banding patterns.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a healthy person shows 46 chromosomes with no visible structural abnormalities. What can be concluded from the karyotype alone?
questions.correct: No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
distractors: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
questions.why: A karyotype detects chromosome number and large structure, not allele sequences; the second distractor wrongly equates homologous chromosomes with identical alleles.
options: The person cannot carry any recessive alleles because both homologs look normal.
Crossing over did not occur during the meiosis that produced the person's gametes.
No chromosome-number or large structural abnormality was detected, but a single-gene mutation could still be present.
All alleles on the person's homologous chromosomes must be identical.

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and is then fertilized. What completes meiosis II, and what cells are produced?
questions.correct: Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.
distractors: Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
questions.why: The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and completes only after sperm entry, with unequal cytokinesis yielding one ovum and a polar body; the first distractor assumes four ova.
options: Meiosis II completes before fertilization, producing two ova from the secondary oocyte.
Ovulation triggers completion, producing four ova from the secondary oocyte.
Fertilization blocks meiosis II, so the first polar body becomes the ovum.
Sperm entry triggers completion, producing one ovum and a second polar body.

questions.stem: In a moss, the green leafy gametophyte is haploid and produces gametes, while the diploid sporophyte produces spores. Which statement correctly explains how these cells are made?
questions.correct: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
distractors: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.
questions.why: Mitosis in an already haploid gametophyte preserves n, while meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores; the second distractor assumes any haploid product requires meiosis.
options: The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.
The haploid gametophyte makes gametes by meiosis, and the diploid sporophyte makes spores by mitosis.
Both gametes and spores are made by meiosis because both are haploid cells.
Both gametes and spores are made by mitosis because both are single cells.

questions.stem: A human zygote with 46 chromosomes divides repeatedly to form an embryo, and later some adult gonadal cells undergo meiosis. Which pairing correctly describes the two divisions?
questions.correct: Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
distractors: Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
questions.why: Mitosis supports growth with the same diploid set, and meiosis produces haploid gametes; the third distractor swaps the roles of the two divisions.
options: Meiosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while mitosis produces gametes.
Mitosis maintains the diploid number in body cells, while meiosis halves it to produce haploid gametes.
Both divisions reduce the chromosome number by half in each daughter cell.
Mitosis halves the chromosome number, while meiosis doubles it before fertilization.

questions.stem: At metaphase I, a human cell has 23 bivalents, or tetrads. What does each bivalent contain?
questions.correct: Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
distractors: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
questions.why: A bivalent is a paired homologous pair, and each homolog is duplicated, giving four chromatids; the first distractor confuses sister chromatids with homologs.
options: Two sister chromatids from one chromosome, for two chromatids total.
One autosome and one sex chromosome, for two chromosomes total.
Two homologous chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, for four chromatids total.
Four homologous chromosomes, each with one chromatid, for four chromosomes total.

questions.stem: A human primary spermatocyte with 46 chromosomes completes meiosis and cytokinesis normally. How many sperm are produced, and what chromosome number does each carry?
questions.correct: Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.
distractors: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
questions.why: Spermatogenesis uses equal cytokinesis after meiosis, yielding four haploid sperm; the last distractor incorrectly applies oogenesis polar-body formation to sperm production.
options: Two sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
Four sperm, each with 46 chromosomes.
One sperm with 23 chromosomes and three polar bodies.
Four sperm, each with 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A population of aphids reproduces asexually, producing genetically identical offspring. A related population reproduces sexually. A new pesticide is applied. Which population is more likely to survive, and why?
questions.correct: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
distractors: The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
questions.why: Sexual reproduction produces variation that may include resistant phenotypes; the first distractor wrongly assumes identical clones are all resistant.
options: The sexual population, because meiosis and fertilization generate varied offspring, some of which may resist the pesticide.
Neither population, because genetic variation cannot affect survival under pesticide exposure.
The asexual population, because asexual reproduction creates new mutations faster than sexual reproduction.
The asexual population, because identical offspring are uniformly resistant to the pesticide.

questions.stem: In many fungi, the zygote is the only diploid cell and undergoes meiosis immediately. How does this differ from the human life cycle?
questions.correct: Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
distractors: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.
questions.why: Fungal zygotes undergo meiosis, leaving mostly haploid stages, while human zygotes grow by mitosis into a diploid body; the last distractor swaps gamete production in the two groups.
options: Fungi spend most of the life cycle diploid, while humans spend most of it haploid.
Fungi spend most of the life cycle haploid, while humans spend most of it diploid and grow from the zygote by mitosis.
Both fungi and humans have multicellular haploid and diploid stages of equal size.
Fungi produce gametes by meiosis, while humans produce gametes by mitosis.

questions.stem: In one bivalent, a single crossover occurs between two nonsister chromatids at a point between genes A and B. After meiosis, how many of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination of A and B alleles?
questions.correct: Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
distractors: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
questions.why: A single crossover involves two nonsister chromatids, producing two recombinant and two parental chromatids; the all-four distractor ignores that sisters not involved remain parental.
options: One of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.
All four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
Two of the four gametes carry a recombinant combination.
None of the four gametes carries a recombinant combination.

questions.stem: A plant cell has 2n = 12 and proceeds through meiosis. At metaphase I, how many tetrads (bivalents) line up at the cell's equatorial plane?
questions.correct: 6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair
distractors: 12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
questions.why: A tetrad is a paired set of homologs, so the count equals the haploid number n = 6; the 12 answer mistakes chromosome count for tetrad count.
options: 24 tetrads, because each chromatid forms a tetrad
12 tetrads, because each chromosome forms its own tetrad
3 tetrads, because the chromosome number is halved first
6 tetrads, because each tetrad is one homologous pair

questions.stem: A human gamete carries two copies of chromosome 7, and the two copies are identical sister chromatids with the same alleles. In which meiotic division did nondisjunction most likely occur?
questions.correct: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
distractors: Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg
questions.why: Homologs separate in meiosis I, so identical sister chromatids reaching one gamete point to meiosis II nondisjunction; the meiosis I distractor assumes all nondisjunction happens when homologs separate.
options: Meiosis II, because sister chromatids failed to separate
Meiosis I, because homologous chromosomes failed to separate
Mitosis before meiosis, because the chromosome replicated twice
Fertilization, because two sperm fused with one egg

questions.stem: In human oogenesis, one primary oocyte produces one large ovum and smaller polar bodies. What is the main reason only one cell normally becomes the functional gamete?
questions.correct: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
distractors: Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
questions.why: Polar bodies are haploid but receive little cytoplasm and degenerate; the diploid distractor confuses small size with an abnormal chromosome number.
options: Polar bodies are diploid and cannot be fertilized
Unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm and nutrients in one cell
Only the ovum completes DNA replication before meiosis
Polar bodies contain the wrong number of chromosomes

questions.stem: During prophase I, a chiasma forms within a tetrad. Which chromatids exchange segments to produce recombinant chromosomes?
questions.correct: Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Sister chromatids of the same chromosome
Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
questions.why: Crossing over joins nonsister chromatids from the two homologs, creating new allele combinations; exchange between sisters would not recombine different alleles.
options: Two chromatids from nonhomologous chromosomes
Two sister chromatids from the same homolog
Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Sister chromatids of the same chromosome

questions.stem: In a human male karyotype, the X and Y chromosomes differ in size and gene content. What happens to X and Y during meiosis I?
questions.correct: They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles
distractors: They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
questions.why: X and Y share homologous pairing regions, so they synapse and separate in meiosis I; the independent-assortment distractor wrongly treats them as unpaired nonhomologs.
options: They replicate again and form two identical X-Y pairs
They are treated as nonhomologs and assort independently of each other
They fail to pair and both move to the same pole
They pair as homologous chromosomes and separate to opposite poles

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 8 proceeds through meiosis. How many chromosomes are present in the whole cell at anaphase I and at anaphase II, respectively?
questions.correct: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
distractors: 8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
questions.why: At anaphase I homologs separate but remain in one cell; at anaphase II sister chromatids separate, doubling the chromosome count in that cell back to 8.
options: 8 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
16 at anaphase I and 8 at anaphase II
8 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II
4 at anaphase I and 4 at anaphase II

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, but one chromosome 5 is visibly shorter than its homolog. Which conclusion is best supported by this karyotype alone?
questions.correct: A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
distractors: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5
questions.why: A karyotype resolves chromosome structure and number, so a shortened homolog indicates a deletion; the point-mutation distractor wrongly assumes karyotypes can show single-base changes.
options: A point mutation has changed one gene on chromosome 5
A structural deletion has removed a piece of one chromosome 5
The cell is haploid for chromosome 5
Nondisjunction produced an extra chromosome 5

questions.stem: A mutant cell destroys centromeric cohesin at the start of anaphase I instead of waiting until anaphase II. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
distractors: Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation
questions.why: Centromeric cohesin holds sister chromatids together until meiosis II; removing it early lets sisters separate in meiosis I, while the homolog-failure distractor confuses cohesin with chiasmata.
options: Crossing over occurs twice in each tetrad
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I
Sister chromatids separate prematurely during meiosis I
The cell completes meiosis I without any chromosome segregation

questions.stem: A human female's primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I until puberty. Which event has not yet occurred in these arrested cells?
questions.correct: Separation of homologous chromosomes
distractors: Replication of DNA before meiosis
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
questions.why: Prophase I arrest occurs after replication, synapsis, and crossing over but before homolog separation; the DNA-replication distractor ignores that S phase precedes the arrest.
options: Crossing over between nonsister chromatids
Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Replication of DNA before meiosis
Separation of homologous chromosomes

questions.stem: A haploid fungus produces gametes by mitosis. Why can this haploid cell not carry out meiosis?
questions.correct: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
distractors: Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
questions.why: Meiosis separates homologs, so a cell with only one set cannot perform the pairing and segregation of meiosis I; the centromere distractor confuses haploidy with loss of chromosome structures.
options: Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair and segregate
Haploid cells have no centromeres to attach to spindle fibers
Haploid cells cannot replicate their DNA before division
Meiosis requires twice as much cytoplasm as mitosis

questions.stem: A human karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, including one X and no Y. Which description of this chromosome set is correct?
questions.correct: Female with monosomy X
distractors: Male with monosomy X
Female with trisomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
questions.why: One X and no Y indicates female sex, and 45 chromosomes means one chromosome is missing; the male distractor assumes a Y must be present for male development or misreads the count.
options: Male with monosomy X
Female with monosomy X
Male with a normal chromosome number
Female with trisomy X

questions.stem: A karyotype from a human shows 47 chromosomes: two X chromosomes, one Y chromosome, and the rest autosomes. How many autosomes are present?
questions.correct: 44 autosomes
distractors: 45 autosomes
46 autosomes
22 autosomes
questions.why: Humans normally have 44 autosomes; the extra chromosome here is a sex chromosome. Counting the Y as an autosome gives 46.
options: 22 autosomes
45 autosomes
44 autosomes
46 autosomes

questions.stem: White blood cells are arrested in metaphase for karyotyping. One treated human cell contains 46 chromosomes. How many DNA molecules and centromeres are present in that cell?
questions.correct: 92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
distractors: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
questions.why: After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids but one centromere, so 46 chromosomes carry 92 DNA molecules. Equating chromatids with centromeres gives 92 centromeres.
options: 46 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 92 centromeres
23 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres
92 DNA molecules and 46 centromeres

questions.stem: A human secondary oocyte is fertilized and completes meiosis II. What chromosome content does the second polar body receive?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
distractors: 23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
questions.why: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, so the second polar body gets one chromatid per chromosome. Leaving chromosomes duplicated confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: 23 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
46 chromosomes, each a single chromatid
23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids

questions.stem: In one tetrad, two nonsister chromatids exchange segments in a single crossover. Before the crossover, two chromatids had paternal centromeres. How many chromatids have paternal centromeres after the crossover?
questions.why: Crossing over swaps distal segments but not centromeres, so two chromatids remain paternal. Assuming the crossover alters every chromatid gives 4.

questions.stem: A triploid plant has three homologs for each chromosome. Why does meiosis usually fail to produce balanced gametes?
questions.correct: Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
distractors: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.
questions.why: Meiosis requires homologs to pair and separate; an odd number leaves unpaired chromosomes and uneven segregation. Blaming DNA replication rather than homolog pairing is a common substitution.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate because centromeres do not split.
Crossing over cannot occur without exactly two homologs.
Homologs cannot pair and segregate evenly, so gametes get variable chromosome numbers.
Fertilization cannot occur because the plant's gametes are diploid.

questions.stem: In a mutant cell with 2n = 8, meiosis I chromosome segregation is normal, but cytokinesis after meiosis I fails. What is the immediate result?
questions.correct: One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.
distractors: One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
questions.why: Chromosomes segregate into two haploid nuclei, but the cell does not divide, so both nuclei remain in one cell. The two-cell result describes normal cytokinesis.
options: Four haploid nuclei, each with 2 chromosomes.
One diploid nucleus with 8 chromosomes.
Two haploid cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
One cell containing two haploid nuclei, each with 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A human spermatogonium undergoes one mitotic division, and both daughter cells immediately complete meiosis. How many sperm are produced?
questions.correct: 8 sperm
distractors: 4 sperm
2 sperm
16 sperm
questions.why: One spermatogonium gives two primary spermatocytes, and each primary spermatocyte yields four sperm. Forgetting the mitotic division gives 4; doubling twice gives 16.
options: 8 sperm
2 sperm
4 sperm
16 sperm

questions.stem: A mutant prevents cleavage of cohesin along chromosome arms in meiosis I but leaves centromeric cohesin protected normally. What is the most likely result?
questions.correct: Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
distractors: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
questions.why: Arm cohesin holds homologs together until anaphase I; without its cleavage, homologs cannot separate. The premature-sister result confuses arm cohesin with centromeric cohesin.
options: Sister chromatids separate prematurely in anaphase I.
Homologs remain joined and fail to separate in anaphase I.
Meiosis II is skipped entirely.
Crossing over occurs twice as often.

questions.stem: A human zygote has 47 chromosomes, including three X chromosomes and no Y. The sperm that fertilized it carried one X. What chromosome content did the egg have?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
distractors: 23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
questions.why: The zygote's extra X must have come from the egg, so the egg carried 22 autosomes plus two X chromosomes. An egg with one X would produce a 46,XX zygote.
options: 23 chromosomes, including no X chromosome.
24 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.
23 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes.
23 chromosomes, including one X chromosome.

questions.stem: A human egg with 24 chromosomes is fertilized by a sperm with 22 chromosomes. The zygote has 46 chromosomes. Why is it still considered aneuploid?
questions.correct: It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.
distractors: It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
questions.why: Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome set, not just an abnormal total; the extra and missing chromosomes unbalance the zygote. Counting total chromosomes only would call it normal diploid.
options: It is triploid because three chromosome sets are present.
It has 46 chromosomes, so it is a normal diploid.
It is haploid because both gametes were abnormal.
It has an extra copy of one chromosome and is missing another, so the set is unbalanced.

questions.stem: A drug prevents spindle formation during meiosis II of a fertilized human secondary oocyte. What is the most direct consequence?
questions.correct: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
distractors: Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
questions.why: Meiosis II uses a spindle to separate sister chromatids; without it, the ovum and polar body are not produced. The homolog-separation result confuses meiosis II with meiosis I.
options: Sister chromatids cannot separate, so a haploid ovum and second polar body cannot form.
The zygote immediately becomes triploid.
Homologs fail to separate, so the oocyte remains diploid.
Crossing over occurs twice as often in prophase II.

questions.stem: A human egg contains two copies of chromosome 1. One copy has a centromere variant inherited from the woman's father, and the other has the variant inherited from her mother. In which division did nondisjunction most likely occur?
questions.correct: Meiosis I, because homologous centromeres failed to separate.
distractors: Meiosis II, because sister centromeres failed to separate.
Mitosis in the oogonium, because homologs failed to separate.
Fertilization, because two sperm centromeres entered the egg.
questions.why: Two different homolog centromeres in one egg mean the homologous pair cosegregated at meiosis I; a meiosis II error would duplicate one sister centromere, not combine both homologs. The meiosis II distractor assumes any extra chromosome comes from sister chromatids.
options: Meiosis I, because homologous centromeres failed to separate.
Fertilization, because two sperm centromeres entered the egg.
Meiosis II, because sister centromeres failed to separate.
Mitosis in the oogonium, because homologs failed to separate.

questions.stem: Genes A and B are on the same chromosome. In 30% of meioses, exactly one crossover occurs between A and B; no double crossovers occur. What percentage of all gametes produced is recombinant for A and B?
questions.why: Each crossover between nonsister chromatids makes two recombinant and two parental chromatids, so 30% of meioses yields 0.30 × 50% = 15% recombinant gametes. Choosing 30% confuses crossover frequency with recombinant gamete frequency.

questions.stem: An organism is heterozygous for three genes on different chromosome pairs: AaBbCc. How many genetically distinct gamete genotypes can it produce through independent assortment?
questions.why: Each of the three heterozygous pairs can contribute either allele independently, giving 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 gamete genotypes. Choosing 3 counts genes rather than allele combinations.

questions.stem: A plant cell with 2n = 18 is at metaphase I of meiosis. How many chromatids are present in the entire cell?
questions.why: After S phase, each of the 18 chromosomes has two sister chromatids, so the cell contains 36 chromatids at metaphase I. Choosing 18 counts chromosomes and ignores replication.

questions.stem: Four gametes produced by normal meiosis from one meiocyte each contain 12 chromosomes. What was the diploid chromosome number of the meiocyte?
questions.why: Normal meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes with 12 chromosomes come from a diploid meiocyte with 24. Choosing 12 mistakes the haploid number for the diploid number.

questions.stem: A tetraploid plant has 4n = 28. Assuming meiosis produces gametes with half the somatic chromosome number, how many chromosomes are in each gamete?
questions.why: Half of 28 is 14, so each gamete receives 14 chromosomes. Choosing 7 incorrectly halves the number twice by treating the plant as diploid.

questions.stem: In a human ovary, 12 secondary oocytes are each fertilized and complete meiosis II normally. How many functional ova and second polar bodies are produced?
questions.correct: 12 ova and 12 second polar bodies
distractors: 12 ova and 24 second polar bodies
24 ova and 12 second polar bodies
6 ova and 6 second polar bodies
questions.why: Each secondary oocyte divides once at meiosis II, yielding one ovum and one second polar body. The 24-polar-body distractor incorrectly counts the first polar body division as a second polar body from each oocyte.
options: 24 ova and 12 second polar bodies
6 ova and 6 second polar bodies
12 ova and 12 second polar bodies
12 ova and 24 second polar bodies

questions.stem: In a moss, a haploid gametophyte has 10 chromosomes. After fertilization, the sporophyte undergoes meiosis to produce spores. How many chromosomes does each spore carry?
questions.why: The sporophyte is diploid with 20 chromosomes, and meiosis halves that to 10 in each spore. Choosing 20 stops before meiosis and gives the sporophyte number.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 6 completes prophase I, but one bivalent forms no chiasma between its homologs. What is the most likely consequence for that homolog pair during meiosis?
questions.correct: The homologs may fail to separate correctly at anaphase I.
distractors: Sister chromatids will separate at anaphase I instead of anaphase II.
The homolog pair will replicate again before meiosis II.
Both homologs will be packaged into the same gamete every time.
questions.why: Chiasmata help hold homologs together and orient them for segregation; without a chiasma, that pair is prone to nondisjunction at meiosis I. The sister-chromatid distractor confuses meiotic anaphase I with anaphase II.
options: The homologs may fail to separate correctly at anaphase I.
Sister chromatids will separate at anaphase I instead of anaphase II.
Both homologs will be packaged into the same gamete every time.
The homolog pair will replicate again before meiosis II.

questions.stem: A technician arranges a normal male's 46 chromosomes by size and centromere position. After separating out the sex chromosomes, how many autosomes remain, and how many homologous pairs of autosomes are there?
questions.correct: 44 autosomes in 22 pairs
distractors: 44 autosomes in 23 pairs
46 autosomes in 23 pairs
22 autosomes in 22 pairs
questions.why: A normal male has 44 autosomes plus X and Y; the 44 autosomes form 22 homologous pairs. The 23-pair distractor includes the sex chromosome pair among autosomes.
options: 44 autosomes in 23 pairs
44 autosomes in 22 pairs
22 autosomes in 22 pairs
46 autosomes in 23 pairs

questions.unit: Crossing over and meiosis I segregation
questions.stem: In a meiocyte, one crossover occurs between two nonsister chromatids within a single tetrad, and the centromeres are not exchanged. The cell then completes meiosis I. What does each of the two daughter cells contain with respect to that crossover?
questions.correct: One recombinant chromatid, because the two exchanged chromatids are attached to centromeres of different homologs, which separate in anaphase I.
distractors: Two recombinant chromatids, because sister chromatids remain together and move to the same pole during meiosis I.
No recombinant chromatids, because crossovers are not resolved until the sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
One recombinant chromatid in only one daughter cell, because both exchanged chromatids are pulled to the same pole at anaphase I.
questions.why: The two exchanged chromatids are nonsister chromatids on different homologs, so homolog separation in anaphase I places one recombinant chromatid in each daughter cell. The distractors exploit the misconception that sister chromatids stay together and therefore must cosegregate.
options: Two recombinant chromatids, because sister chromatids remain together and move to the same pole during meiosis I.
No recombinant chromatids, because crossovers are not resolved until the sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
One recombinant chromatid, because the two exchanged chromatids are attached to centromeres of different homologs, which separate in anaphase I.
One recombinant chromatid in only one daughter cell, because both exchanged chromatids are pulled to the same pole at anaphase I.

questions.stem: In a sample of 200 lily meiocytes, 90 are in prophase I, 30 in metaphase I, 10 in anaphase I, and 70 in telophase II. Which conclusion about the meiotic divisions is best supported?
questions.correct: Prophase I occupies more of the meiotic time than any other stage listed.
distractors: Anaphase I lasts longer than prophase I in these cells.
Telophase II occurs before metaphase I in the meiotic sequence.
The cells complete meiosis in the order prophase I, telophase II, metaphase I, anaphase I.
questions.why: The stage with the most cells is the longest, since random sampling catches more cells there; anaphase I is the least frequent, not the longest.
options: Anaphase I lasts longer than prophase I in these cells.
The cells complete meiosis in the order prophase I, telophase II, metaphase I, anaphase I.
Telophase II occurs before metaphase I in the meiotic sequence.
Prophase I occupies more of the meiotic time than any other stage listed.

questions.stem: A table shows relative DNA per cell in human spermatogenesis: spermatogonium 2.0, primary spermatocyte 4.0, secondary spermatocyte 2.0, spermatid 1.0. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: DNA is replicated before meiosis I, and each meiotic division halves the DNA per cell.
distractors: DNA is replicated between meiosis I and meiosis II, producing the secondary spermatocyte value.
The secondary spermatocyte has twice the DNA of a spermatogonium.
The spermatid is diploid because its DNA content is 1.0.
questions.why: The rise from 2.0 to 4.0 happens before meiosis I, and the drops to 2.0 then 1.0 show the two divisions halving DNA; replication between divisions is the common error.
options: DNA is replicated before meiosis I, and each meiotic division halves the DNA per cell.
The spermatid is diploid because its DNA content is 1.0.
DNA is replicated between meiosis I and meiosis II, producing the secondary spermatocyte value.
The secondary spermatocyte has twice the DNA of a spermatogonium.

questions.stem: In Sordaria, asci with spores in a 4:4 pattern are parental, while 2:2:2:2 and 2:4:2 patterns are recombinant. A sample of 100 asci contains 60 parental and 40 recombinant asci. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Crossing over between the gene and the centromere occurred in some meioses.
distractors: No crossing over occurred because most asci are parental.
Independent assortment alone produced the 4:4 asci.
Every spore in the recombinant asci carries a new mutation.
questions.why: Recombinant spore patterns arise when a crossover occurs between the gene and the centromere; a parental majority does not mean crossing over was absent.
options: No crossing over occurred because most asci are parental.
Crossing over between the gene and the centromere occurred in some meioses.
Independent assortment alone produced the 4:4 asci.
Every spore in the recombinant asci carries a new mutation.

questions.stem: In a mapping cross, recombination frequencies are A-B 10%, B-C 15%, and A-C 5%. Which gene order is most consistent with these data?
questions.correct: B-A-C
distractors: A-B-C
A-C-B
C-B-A
questions.why: The largest recombination frequency is between B and C, and it roughly equals A-B plus A-C, so A lies between B and C.
options: A-B-C
C-B-A
B-A-C
A-C-B

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 8 is observed at four times. At time 1 it has 8 chromosomes and 16 chromatids; time 2, 4 chromosomes and 8 chromatids; time 3, 8 chromosomes and 8 chromatids; time 4, 4 chromosomes and 4 chromatids. Which time corresponds to anaphase II?
questions.correct: Time 3
distractors: Time 1
Time 2
Time 4
questions.why: At anaphase II sister chromatids have separated, giving 8 single-chromatid chromosomes and 8 chromatids; time 2 is metaphase II and time 4 is a gamete.
options: Time 2
Time 4
Time 1
Time 3

questions.stem: A meiocyte with 2n = 12 is followed through meiosis. Before meiosis I it has 12 chromosomes; each daughter after meiosis I has 6; each gamete after meiosis II has 6. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Meiosis I is the reductional division because it halves chromosome number, while meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
distractors: Meiosis II is reductional because it produces four cells.
Chromosome number is halved only at fertilization.
DNA replication between the divisions explains the drop from 12 to 6.
questions.why: The chromosome count falls from 12 to 6 at meiosis I, so that division is reductional; meiosis II keeps the number at 6 while separating sister chromatids.
options: Meiosis I is the reductional division because it halves chromosome number, while meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Chromosome number is halved only at fertilization.
Meiosis II is reductional because it produces four cells.

questions.stem: A researcher counts chiasmata in 100 tetrads: 50 tetrads have no chiasma, 40 have one, and 10 have two. Which conclusion about crossing over is best supported?

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, but a segment of chromosome 8 has moved to chromosome 14 and a segment of 14 has moved to 8; no chromosome material is visibly missing. Which conclusion is best supported?
