Two cells, each containing two diploid nuclei.
questions.why: Meiosis II still partitions chromatids into four haploid nuclei, but without cytokinesis II the two secondary cells each retain two nuclei; the misconception is that nuclear division and cell division are the same.
options: One cell containing four diploid nuclei.
Four separate haploid cells, each with one nucleus.
Two cells, each containing two haploid nuclei.
Two cells, each containing two diploid nuclei.

questions.stem: In Drosophila, recombination between two linked genes is 12% in females and 0% in males. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Crossing over between these genes occurs in females but not in males.
distractors: The genes are on different chromosomes in females but linked in males.
Male Drosophila have no homologous chromosomes.
Recombination frequency cannot be compared between sexes.
questions.why: The data directly show sex-specific crossing over; the misconception is that 0% recombination means the genes must be unlinked or that males lack homologs.
options: Recombination frequency cannot be compared between sexes.
Male Drosophila have no homologous chromosomes.
The genes are on different chromosomes in females but linked in males.
Crossing over between these genes occurs in females but not in males.

questions.stem: A table lists four human cells by chromosome number and centromere number. Which row represents a secondary spermatocyte at anaphase II?
questions.correct: 46 chromosomes, 46 centromeres
distractors: 23 chromosomes, 23 centromeres
46 chromosomes, 23 centromeres
23 chromosomes, 46 centromeres
questions.why: At anaphase II centromeres split, so the 23 replicated chromosomes become 46 single-chromatid chromosomes; the misconception is that anaphase II still has 23 centromeres.
options: 46 chromosomes, 46 centromeres
46 chromosomes, 23 centromeres
23 chromosomes, 46 centromeres
23 chromosomes, 23 centromeres

questions.stem: A species has 2n = 6. Each parent can produce 2^3 = 8 kinds of gametes by independent assortment. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically distinct zygote chromosome combinations can random fertilization produce?
questions.why: Each of 8 egg types can combine with each of 8 sperm types, giving 8 × 8 = 64; the misconception is adding gamete types instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Unequal crossing over occurs between two nonsister chromatids in a tetrad, so one recombinant chromatid gains a segment and the other loses it. Which outcome is most likely after meiosis?
questions.correct: Two gametes carry a duplication and a deletion, respectively; the other two are normal.
distractors: All four gametes carry the deletion.
The cell cannot complete meiosis.
Both recombinant gametes carry duplications.
questions.why: Unequal crossing over creates reciprocal duplication/deletion chromatids; the misconception is that crossing over always exchanges equal segments.
options: All four gametes carry the deletion.
Both recombinant gametes carry duplications.
Two gametes carry a duplication and a deletion, respectively; the other two are normal.
The cell cannot complete meiosis.

questions.stem: A dihybrid testcross yields only two phenotypic classes, each about half of the offspring, with no recombinant classes observed. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The two genes are completely linked and no crossing over was detected.
distractors: The two genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
The two genes are 50 map units apart.
One gene is epistatic to the other.
questions.why: Only parental combinations appear, so the genes are linked with no observed recombination; the misconception is that a 1:1 ratio always means independent assortment.
options: One gene is epistatic to the other.
The two genes are 50 map units apart.
The two genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
The two genes are completely linked and no crossing over was detected.

questions.stem: A plant is exposed to increasing light intensity while CO2 and temperature are held constant. Oxygen production rises until 800 units of light, then stays flat. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Light is no longer limiting; some other factor limits the rate.
distractors: The plant has stopped photosynthesizing.
Respiration has stopped.
Oxygen production will rise if light increases further.
questions.why: The plateau indicates a different limiting factor such as CO2; the misconception is that more light always increases photosynthesis.
options: Light is no longer limiting; some other factor limits the rate.
The plant has stopped photosynthesizing.
Respiration has stopped.
Oxygen production will rise if light increases further.

questions.stem: Germinating pea seeds consume 2.0 mL O2/min at 20°C and 3.0 mL O2/min at 30°C. What is the Q10 for this temperature range?
questions.why: Q10 is rate at T + 10 divided by rate at T, so 3.0/2.0 = 1.5; the misconception is that Q10 is the difference or a percent.

questions.stem: An enzyme is assayed with and without an inhibitor. At high substrate concentration, the inhibited reaction reaches the same Vmax as the uninhibited reaction, but its Km is higher. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The inhibitor is competitive.
distractors: The inhibitor is noncompetitive.
The inhibitor denatures the enzyme.
The inhibitor lowers Vmax.
questions.why: Competitive inhibitors raise Km but do not change Vmax; the misconception is that any inhibitor lowers Vmax.
options: The inhibitor denatures the enzyme.
The inhibitor lowers Vmax.
The inhibitor is competitive.
The inhibitor is noncompetitive.

questions.stem: Cells grown in 15N are shifted to 14N medium. After one round, all DNA molecules are hybrid; after two rounds, half are hybrid and half are light. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: DNA replication is semiconservative.
distractors: DNA replication is conservative.
DNA replication is dispersive.
DNA replication is conservative in the first round only.
questions.why: The pattern of hybrid and light molecules matches semiconservative replication; the misconception is that conservative replication would keep one fully heavy molecule.
options: DNA replication is conservative in the first round only.
DNA replication is dispersive.
DNA replication is conservative.
DNA replication is semiconservative.

questions.stem: A population of paramecia grows rapidly in a culture, then levels off at about 500 individuals even though nutrients are still present. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The population has reached carrying capacity.
distractors: The population is growing exponentially.
The population has no limiting factors.
The population will continue to double each day.
questions.why: The plateau at a stable size indicates carrying capacity; the misconception is that unlimited nutrients mean unlimited growth.
options: The population has reached carrying capacity.
The population will continue to double each day.
The population has no limiting factors.
The population is growing exponentially.

questions.stem: A human sperm is found to carry both an X and a Y chromosome, along with 22 autosomes. Which meiotic error most directly explains this sperm?
questions.correct: Nondisjunction of the X and Y homologs during meiosis I.
distractors: Nondisjunction of sister chromatids during meiosis II.
Failure of cytokinesis after meiosis II.
Fertilization of an egg by two sperm.
questions.why: X and Y are homologs and normally separate in meiosis I, so a sperm carrying both reflects meiosis I nondisjunction, not meiosis II sister-chromatid failure.
options: Nondisjunction of the X and Y homologs during meiosis I.
Failure of cytokinesis after meiosis II.
Fertilization of an egg by two sperm.
Nondisjunction of sister chromatids during meiosis II.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte completes meiosis I. The first polar body does not divide, but the secondary oocyte is fertilized and completes meiosis II. How many cells are produced, and what is their chromosome number?
questions.correct: One ovum and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
distractors: One ovum and one polar body, each with 23 chromosomes.
Two ova and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum with 46 chromosomes and two polar bodies with 23 chromosomes.
questions.why: The first polar body persists as a haploid cell, and meiosis II adds a second polar body, leaving one haploid ovum with 23 chromosomes.
options: One ovum and one polar body, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
Two ova and two polar bodies, each with 23 chromosomes.
One ovum with 46 chromosomes and two polar bodies with 23 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A human primary oocyte has genotype AaBb, with the A and B genes on different chromosome pairs. After meiosis I, the secondary oocyte carries A and b. Ignoring crossing over, what does the first polar body carry?
questions.correct: a and B, because homologs of both pairs segregated to opposite poles.
distractors: A and B, because the polar body receives the sister chromatids of both chromosomes.
a and b, because independent assortment randomizes which alleles stay together.
A and b, because sister chromatids separate during meiosis I.
questions.why: Meiosis I separates homologs, not sister chromatids, so the polar body receives the other homolog of each pair: a and B.
options: A and b, because sister chromatids separate during meiosis I.
a and b, because independent assortment randomizes which alleles stay together.
a and B, because homologs of both pairs segregated to opposite poles.
A and B, because the polar body receives the sister chromatids of both chromosomes.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 10 proceeds through meiosis. At anaphase I, how many chromosomes are moving toward each pole, and how many chromatids does each of those chromosomes have?
questions.correct: 5 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
distractors: 10 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
10 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
questions.why: Anaphase I separates homologs, so each pole receives one chromosome from each of the five pairs, and each chromosome is still duplicated.
options: 10 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids
10 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 1 chromatid
5 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids

questions.stem: A human male produces 400 sperm by normal meiosis. On average, how many of these sperm carry a Y chromosome?
questions.correct: 200 sperm
distractors: 0 sperm
100 sperm
400 sperm
questions.why: X and Y separate in meiosis I, so half the sperm receive Y and half receive X, giving about 200 Y-bearing sperm.
options: 200 sperm
0 sperm
400 sperm
100 sperm

questions.stem: A chloroplast is illuminated with light, and then CO2 is suddenly removed from its surroundings. Which immediate change is expected?
questions.correct: ATP and NADPH accumulate, and O2 production continues briefly because the light reactions do not require CO2.
distractors: O2 production stops immediately because CO2 is the final electron acceptor.
ATP and NADPH production stops immediately because the Calvin cycle cannot use them.
Water splitting stops immediately because NADP+ is no longer available.
questions.why: CO2 is used in the Calvin cycle, not the light reactions; without it, ATP and NADPH build up while water splitting continues briefly.
options: O2 production stops immediately because CO2 is the final electron acceptor.
ATP and NADPH accumulate, and O2 production continues briefly because the light reactions do not require CO2.
ATP and NADPH production stops immediately because the Calvin cycle cannot use them.
Water splitting stops immediately because NADP+ is no longer available.

questions.stem: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. What is the most likely immediate effect on a respiring cell?
questions.correct: ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases because the proton gradient is lost.
distractors: O2 consumption stops immediately because electrons can no longer flow.
Glycolysis stops immediately because NADH cannot be oxidized.
ATP synthesis increases because protons reach ATP synthase more easily.
questions.why: The proton gradient drives ATP synthase; a leak dissipates it, so ATP synthesis falls even though electron transport may continue.
options: ATP synthesis increases because protons reach ATP synthase more easily.
O2 consumption stops immediately because electrons can no longer flow.
ATP synthesis by ATP synthase decreases because the proton gradient is lost.
Glycolysis stops immediately because NADH cannot be oxidized.

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next child will be affected?
questions.why: Both parents must be carriers, and each child has a 1/4 chance of inheriting two recessive alleles; the prior affected child does not change the next child's odds.

questions.stem: In a food chain, producers fix 50,000 kJ of energy. If 10 percent of energy is transferred to each successive trophic level, how much energy is available to the tertiary consumers?
questions.correct: 50 kJ
distractors: 500 kJ
0.5 kJ
questions.why: Energy is multiplied by 0.1 at each of three transfers: 50,000 to primary consumers is 5,000, to secondary consumers 500, and to tertiary consumers 50 kJ.
options: 50 kJ
0.5 kJ
500 kJ

questions.stem: A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from UAC (tyrosine) to UAA. What is the most likely effect on the protein produced?
questions.correct: Translation stops early because UAA is a stop codon.
distractors: One amino acid is replaced by another because the codon still specifies an amino acid.
The reading frame shifts after the mutation, changing all later amino acids.
The mRNA is not transcribed because the mutation affects the promoter.
questions.why: UAA is a nonsense codon, so the ribosome terminates translation prematurely; a substitution would require a codon that still specifies an amino acid.
options: The mRNA is not transcribed because the mutation affects the promoter.
Translation stops early because UAA is a stop codon.
One amino acid is replaced by another because the codon still specifies an amino acid.
The reading frame shifts after the mutation, changing all later amino acids.

questions.stem: One rodent species has 2n = 8 and a related species has 2n = 12; both are heterozygous at every locus. Ignoring crossing over, how many times more gamete chromosome combinations can one individual of the 12-chromosome species produce than one individual of the 8-chromosome species?
questions.correct: Four times as many, since the two species produce 64 and 16 combinations respectively
distractors: Four more combinations, because the species differ by four chromosomes in total
The same number, because both species are diploid and assort independently in the same way
Six times as many, because the larger species has six chromosome pairs
questions.why: Independent assortment yields 2^n gamete combinations, where n is the haploid number: 2^6 = 64 versus 2^4 = 16, a fourfold difference. Subtracting chromosome counts (12 - 8) mistakes chromosomes for the exponent.
options: Six times as many, because the larger species has six chromosome pairs
The same number, because both species are diploid and assort independently in the same way
Four times as many, since the two species produce 64 and 16 combinations respectively
Four more combinations, because the species differ by four chromosomes in total

questions.stem: A diploid germ cell enters meiosis without completing S phase, but its homologs still pair. Which description of a resulting tetrad is most accurate?
questions.correct: It contains two unreplicated chromosomes, so only two chromatids are present instead of four.
distractors: It contains four chromatids because homologs replicate during synapsis.
It contains two chromosomes but four centromeres because centromeres duplicate without DNA replication.
It cannot form a spindle, so homologs never pair.
questions.why: S phase produces sister chromatids; skipping it leaves one chromatid per homolog, so a tetrad has two chromatids. The wrong options assume replication occurs during synapsis or that centromeres duplicate independently.
options: It contains four chromatids because homologs replicate during synapsis.
It cannot form a spindle, so homologs never pair.
It contains two chromosomes but four centromeres because centromeres duplicate without DNA replication.
It contains two unreplicated chromosomes, so only two chromatids are present instead of four.

questions.stem: A physician examines a standard karyotype made from a person's white blood cells and sees 46 normally paired chromosomes. Why can this karyotype not reveal whether crossing over occurred during the person's meiosis?
questions.correct: It shows condensed mitotic chromosomes, not meiotic tetrads, so reciprocal exchanges leave no visible record.
distractors: Crossing over changes chromosome number, which karyotypes cannot detect.
White blood cells never undergo meiosis, so they contain no homologous chromosomes.
Crossing over only occurs in gametes, which are not present in blood.
questions.why: A karyotype uses mitotic metaphase chromosomes; crossing over happens in meiotic prophase I and is reciprocal, so it does not change chromosome number. The wrong options confuse chromosome number with exchange of segments.
options: It shows condensed mitotic chromosomes, not meiotic tetrads, so reciprocal exchanges leave no visible record.
White blood cells never undergo meiosis, so they contain no homologous chromosomes.
Crossing over only occurs in gametes, which are not present in blood.
Crossing over changes chromosome number, which karyotypes cannot detect.

questions.stem: Immediately after a human sperm and egg fuse, the zygote contains 46 chromosomes. What happens to the maternal and paternal homologs at this point?
questions.correct: They remain separate chromosomes in one nucleus and do not pair or cross over until meiosis.
distractors: They immediately pair into 23 tetrads to check for damage.
They fuse into 23 chromosomes, each containing both parental DNA.
They undergo crossing over to create new allele combinations before the first mitosis.
questions.why: Homolog pairing and crossing over occur in prophase I of meiosis, not at fertilization. The wrong options mistakenly treat fertilization as a pairing or recombination event.
options: They undergo crossing over to create new allele combinations before the first mitosis.
They remain separate chromosomes in one nucleus and do not pair or cross over until meiosis.
They fuse into 23 chromosomes, each containing both parental DNA.
They immediately pair into 23 tetrads to check for damage.

questions.stem: A human spermatogonium divides by mitosis, and one daughter enters meiosis while the other remains a stem cell. What is the main advantage of this arrangement?
questions.correct: It maintains a supply of spermatogonia while also producing gametes.
distractors: It doubles the chromosome number before meiosis begins.
It creates genetic variation by crossing over during mitosis.
It ensures every daughter cell becomes a primary oocyte.
questions.why: Mitotic division renews the stem-cell population while meiosis produces sperm. The wrong options confuse mitosis with crossing over or with meiotic chromosome reduction.
options: It creates genetic variation by crossing over during mitosis.
It ensures every daughter cell becomes a primary oocyte.
It maintains a supply of spermatogonia while also producing gametes.
It doubles the chromosome number before meiosis begins.

questions.stem: A karyotype is prepared from a normal human sperm rather than a somatic cell. Which result should the technician expect?
questions.correct: 23 chromosomes, with no homologous pairs present.
distractors: 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs.
23 pairs of chromosomes, including one X and one Y.
46 chromosomes, but only 22 homologous pairs.
questions.why: A sperm is haploid with 23 chromosomes, so it has no homologous pairs. The wrong options incorrectly retain the diploid pairing seen in somatic cells.
options: 23 pairs of chromosomes, including one X and one Y.
46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs.
46 chromosomes, but only 22 homologous pairs.
23 chromosomes, with no homologous pairs present.

questions.stem: Within seconds after one sperm fuses with a human egg, the egg's membrane changes and cortical granules release enzymes that prevent additional sperm from entering. Why is this block essential?
questions.correct: It prevents a zygote with extra chromosome sets, which would disrupt meiosis and development.
distractors: It prevents the egg from completing meiosis II and forming a polar body.
It ensures the zygote receives mitochondria from only the sperm.
It stops crossing over from occurring in the zygote's first mitosis.
questions.why: Polyspermy would create a triploid zygote with extra chromosome sets, disrupting development. The wrong options confuse this block with polar-body formation, mitochondria, or mitosis.
options: It prevents a zygote with extra chromosome sets, which would disrupt meiosis and development.
It prevents the egg from completing meiosis II and forming a polar body.
It ensures the zygote receives mitochondria from only the sperm.
It stops crossing over from occurring in the zygote's first mitosis.

questions.stem: In humans, a sperm contributes a haploid nucleus and a centriole, while the egg contributes a haploid nucleus plus most of the cytoplasm. Why is the egg's large cytoplasmic contribution important after fertilization?
questions.correct: It supplies nutrients and organelles that support early embryonic divisions before implantation.
distractors: It provides a second set of chromosomes that makes the zygote diploid.
It allows the zygote to skip DNA replication before its first mitosis.
It prevents independent assortment during the zygote's first meiotic division.
questions.why: The egg cytoplasm supports early development, but diploidy comes from the two haploid nuclei. The wrong options misattribute chromosome contribution or cell-cycle events to the cytoplasm.
options: It prevents independent assortment during the zygote's first meiotic division.
It supplies nutrients and organelles that support early embryonic divisions before implantation.
It provides a second set of chromosomes that makes the zygote diploid.
It allows the zygote to skip DNA replication before its first mitosis.

questions.stem: At metaphase I, chiasmata hold each pair of homologs together. What must happen to these chiasmata for anaphase I to proceed normally?
questions.correct: They must be released so the homologs can move to opposite poles.
distractors: They must duplicate so each pole receives a chiasma.
They must move to the equator and attach to spindle fibers.
They must form a synaptonemal complex between sister chromatids.
questions.why: Chiasmata are temporary links between homologs; their release allows anaphase I separation. The wrong options treat chiasmata as spindle attachments or as structures that duplicate.
options: They must duplicate so each pole receives a chiasma.
They must move to the equator and attach to spindle fibers.
They must be released so the homologs can move to opposite poles.
They must form a synaptonemal complex between sister chromatids.

questions.stem: During prophase I, two nonsister chromatids break and exchange equal segments. Why does this crossing over usually leave each chromosome with the same overall length and gene content?
questions.correct: The exchange is reciprocal, so the segments swapped between homologs are equal and replace one another.
distractors: The broken ends are repaired by DNA polymerase using the sister chromatid as a template.
The exchanged segments are immediately degraded, leaving the chromosome shorter.
Crossing over duplicates the exchanged segments, increasing gene number on both chromatids.
questions.why: Crossing over is a reciprocal exchange, so equal segments replace one another and length is conserved. The wrong options describe nonreciprocal repair, loss, or duplication.
options: The exchanged segments are immediately degraded, leaving the chromosome shorter.
Crossing over duplicates the exchanged segments, increasing gene number on both chromatids.
The broken ends are repaired by DNA polymerase using the sister chromatid as a template.
The exchange is reciprocal, so the segments swapped between homologs are equal and replace one another.

questions.stem: A cell in G1 has DNA damage. The G1/S checkpoint normally stops the cell from entering S phase. If this checkpoint fails, what is the most likely consequence?
questions.correct: The cell copies damaged DNA and may pass mutations to daughter cells.
distractors: The cell immediately enters mitosis without copying its DNA.
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during anaphase I.
The cell always undergoes apoptosis before replication.
questions.why: Checkpoint failure lets a cell replicate damaged DNA, increasing mutation risk in daughter cells. The wrong options confuse the G1/S checkpoint with mitosis or meiosis and ignore that apoptosis is not guaranteed.
options: The cell copies damaged DNA and may pass mutations to daughter cells.
The cell immediately enters mitosis without copying its DNA.
Homologous chromosomes fail to separate during anaphase I.
The cell always undergoes apoptosis before replication.

questions.stem: In E. coli, a mutation prevents the lac repressor from binding the operator. If glucose is low, what happens to lac operon expression?
questions.correct: The operon is transcribed continuously, even when lactose is absent.
distractors: The operon is transcribed only when lactose is present.
The operon is never transcribed because the promoter is blocked.
The operon is transcribed only when glucose is high.
questions.why: Without repressor binding, the operator cannot block transcription, so lactose is not needed to derepress the operon. The wrong options assume the repressor is still controlling expression.
options: The operon is transcribed only when lactose is present.
The operon is transcribed continuously, even when lactose is absent.
The operon is transcribed only when glucose is high.
The operon is never transcribed because the promoter is blocked.

questions.stem: A table shows chromosome numbers in four tissues of a flowering plant: root 24, leaf 24, pollen grain 12, endosperm 36. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: The endosperm is triploid, consistent with a haploid sperm nucleus fusing with two haploid polar nuclei.
distractors: The pollen grain is diploid because it has half the chromosome number of the root.
The endosperm is haploid because it is produced directly by meiosis.
The root and leaf are haploid because they contain the same number of chromosomes.
questions.why: Root and leaf are diploid (2n = 24), pollen is haploid (n = 12), and endosperm is 3n = 36 after double fertilization; the distractors confuse haploid with half and triploid with haploid.
options: The root and leaf are haploid because they contain the same number of chromosomes.
The endosperm is haploid because it is produced directly by meiosis.
The endosperm is triploid, consistent with a haploid sperm nucleus fusing with two haploid polar nuclei.
The pollen grain is diploid because it has half the chromosome number of the root.

questions.stem: Two linked genes in a plant were scored in testcrosses at two temperatures. Recombination was 8% at 15°C and 16% at 25°C. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Temperature can alter the frequency of crossing over between these linked genes.
distractors: The two genes move to different chromosomes at 25°C.
Independent assortment increases as temperature rises.
Crossing over at 25°C occurred during mitosis rather than meiosis.
questions.why: Recombination between linked genes depends on crossing over in meiosis and can be environmentally modified; the distractors confuse recombination with independent assortment or mitosis.
options: Crossing over at 25°C occurred during mitosis rather than meiosis.
The two genes move to different chromosomes at 25°C.
Independent assortment increases as temperature rises.
Temperature can alter the frequency of crossing over between these linked genes.

questions.stem: In 200 tetrads with two crossovers between the same two loci, 80 yielded two recombinant chromatids, 100 yielded three, and 20 yielded four. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Double crossovers can involve two, three, or four chromatids, so crossover number does not always equal recombinant chromatid number.
distractors: Every double crossover produces four recombinant chromatids.
Crossing over occurs only between sister chromatids.
Recombination frequency always equals the number of crossovers per tetrad.
questions.why: Two crossovers may share a chromatid, leaving some parental combinations; the distractors assume all crossovers are independent or sister-only.
options: Double crossovers can involve two, three, or four chromatids, so crossover number does not always equal recombinant chromatid number.
Recombination frequency always equals the number of crossovers per tetrad.
Crossing over occurs only between sister chromatids.
Every double crossover produces four recombinant chromatids.

questions.stem: A table records chiasmata along chromosome 3 in 100 meiocytes: 60 near the ends, 25 in the middle, and 15 near the centromere. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Crossing over is not uniformly distributed along the chromosome.
distractors: Crossing over occurs only near the chromosome ends.
Chiasmata form during anaphase I.
The centromere is the most frequent site of crossing over.
questions.why: The data show more crossovers near the ends but not exclusively there; chiasmata form in prophase I, not anaphase I.
options: Chiasmata form during anaphase I.
Crossing over is not uniformly distributed along the chromosome.
The centromere is the most frequent site of crossing over.
Crossing over occurs only near the chromosome ends.

questions.stem: A table lists four chromosome pairs from a human karyotype by length and centromere position. Pair 1 is longest and metacentric; Pair 2 is long and submetacentric; Pairs 3 and 4 are short and acrocentric. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: Pairs 3 and 4 cannot be matched as homologs by length and centromere position alone; banding patterns are needed.
distractors: Pair 1 must be the X chromosome pair because it is the longest.
Pairs 3 and 4 are homologous to each other because both are acrocentric.
Centromere position alone is sufficient to identify every homologous pair.
questions.why: Many human chromosomes share size and centromere class, so karyotype pairing relies on banding; the distractors confuse similar appearance with homology.
options: Pairs 3 and 4 are homologous to each other because both are acrocentric.
Pair 1 must be the X chromosome pair because it is the longest.
Pairs 3 and 4 cannot be matched as homologs by length and centromere position alone; banding patterns are needed.
Centromere position alone is sufficient to identify every homologous pair.

questions.stem: A table lists four human ovarian cells: Cell 1 has 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids; Cell 2 has 46 and 92; Cell 3 has 23 and 46; Cell 4 has 23 and 23. Which cell is a secondary oocyte at metaphase II?
questions.correct: Cell 3, with 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
distractors: Cell 1, with 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
Cell 2, with 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
Cell 4, with 23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids.
questions.why: After meiosis I the secondary oocyte is haploid (23) but each chromosome still has two sister chromatids (46); Cell 1 is G1, Cell 2 is primary oocyte after S, and Cell 4 is an ovum.
options: Cell 4, with 23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids.
Cell 2, with 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
Cell 1, with 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
Cell 3, with 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.

questions.stem: A single meiocyte heterozygous at two linked loci produces four gametes with genotypes AB, AB, ab, and ab. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.correct: No crossing over occurred between the two loci in this meiosis.
distractors: The two loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Crossing over occurred between sister chromatids at these loci.
The meiocyte produced four recombinant gametes.
questions.why: Only two gamete genotypes, each duplicated, indicate the alleles stayed linked; independent assortment or crossing over would produce additional recombinant types.
options: No crossing over occurred between the two loci in this meiosis.
The meiocyte produced four recombinant gametes.
The two loci are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Crossing over occurred between sister chromatids at these loci.

questions.stem: A table lists somatic chromosome numbers for four diploid species: Species 1 has 14, Species 2 has 28, Species 3 has 42, and Species 4 has 56. Which species produces gametes with 14 chromosomes?
questions.correct: Species 2, with 28 somatic chromosomes.
distractors: Species 1, with 14 somatic chromosomes.
Species 3, with 42 somatic chromosomes.
Species 4, with 56 somatic chromosomes.
questions.why: Gametes are haploid, so a diploid species with 28 chromosomes produces gametes with 14; the distractors mistake the somatic number for the gamete number or halve the wrong species.
options: Species 1, with 14 somatic chromosomes.
Species 2, with 28 somatic chromosomes.
Species 3, with 42 somatic chromosomes.
Species 4, with 56 somatic chromosomes.

questions.stem: A table lists chromosome contents of four human gametes: Gamete 1 has 22 autosomes + X; Gamete 2 has 22 autosomes + Y; Gamete 3 has 23 autosomes + X; Gamete 4 has 23 autosomes + Y. Which are normal sperm?
questions.correct: Gamete 1 and Gamete 2 only.
distractors: Gamete 3 and Gamete 4 only.
Gamete 1 and Gamete 3 only.
Gamete 2 and Gamete 4 only.
questions.why: A normal sperm is haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome; Gametes 3 and 4 have an extra autosome and are aneuploid.
options: Gamete 1 and Gamete 3 only.
Gamete 2 and Gamete 4 only.
Gamete 1 and Gamete 2 only.
Gamete 3 and Gamete 4 only.

questions.stem: A table shows a family: two unaffected parents have one affected daughter and one unaffected son. No other family history is given. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
questions.correct: Autosomal recessive
distractors: X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
Y-linked
questions.why: Two unaffected parents producing an affected daughter indicate a recessive allele carried by both parents; X-linked recessive is unlikely because an affected daughter would need an affected father.
options: Y-linked
Autosomal dominant
